content:
After years of talking about it, dreaming about it and hoping for it, I now actually have an EPSRC research grant to begin the long journey towards a formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean! I got the official letter confirming this today.

The grant buys out my teaching and administration for 5 years starting October 2024. So right now the project literally does not exist, and will probably continue to be vaporware for at least 6 months, as today I am also embarking upon an intense period of teaching which doesn't lighten up until the beginning of April 2024. But then it really is going to happen :-) I will have time to lead it and having watched Patrick and Johan lead projects, I believe I know what needs to be done.

For reasons related to UK politics I applied for no EPSRC money for PhD students and post-docs, so this grant will not create any new post-doc jobs. However, potential PhD students who want to work with me on this should just apply for a PhD position via Imperial's website in December or so; Imperial have promised me at least one PhD position coming from their own funds, so there will be that.

Earlier this year Adam Topaz and I ran a Copenhagen masterclass on formalisation of (condensed) mathematics and this highly enjoyable week gave rise to many PRs to mathlib, a bunch of small group work, and real progress in mathlib's library for condensed abelian groups. Rather than hiring post-docs to work full-time on the project, I am tempted to now start applying for funds for running workshops like this, where people can hack on one focussed topic with a well-defined goal. Another possibility is internships, where a much smaller group of people come together for a period of two months in the summer and hack on whatever we're up to. I cannot make any concrete statements right now (other than "if anyone knows potential sources of funding then do let me know") but I've already heard positive noises from some sources. Let's wait and see.

I am not at all confident that we will have a full proof of FLT by 2029 when the grant ends. However I am confident that by then we will have succeeded in reducing Fermat's Last Theorem to (possibly super-complex) results which were known to humanity by the 1980s; five years should be plenty of time to define RRR and TTT, write down the map between them, and prove that it's an isomorphism (especially if I can skip everything known by the late 1980s); this R=TR=TR=T idea is the main technique Wiles introduced in his paper and the ideas have been streamlined now. And Lean is very good at commutative algebra.

Once this is done it will be absolutely clear that the project is feasible, and I am hoping that this momentum will somehow get us over the finish line and finish @Freek Wiedijk 's benchmark of 100 formalisation challenges.

I won't bore people here with the technical details of the actual proof I intend to formalise; it is a more modern version of the Taylor-Wiles proof which was created during discussions with Taylor on what would be an optimal route to the summit. There is far less analysis involved than in the original Taylor--Wiles proof (for example no Langlands--Tunnell) but there is still some analysis there (for example multiplicity 1 results for GL_2 over a totally real field). Away from analysis, an example of a big algebraic project which I am going to be not touching, at least at the beginning, is Mazur's theorem from the late 70s classifying the torsion subgroups of elliptic curves over the rationals. Every known proof of FLT (well, every proof known to me) uses Mazur's theorem and I imagine that this will be one of several bottlenecks that we'll run into when formalising the full proof. However I do believe that the top-down approach of breaking the proof into smaller parts and postponing some of them will give the project some momentum.

Let's see what happens!

Thank you to everyone on this Zulip who has supported me and encouraged me to do this over the years. Now it's actually happening and I'm very excited :-)
